title: Section 3
context: Two psychology students, Priya and Callum, are discussing their presentation about background music and concentration with their tutor, Dr Brandt.

audio.t: Section 3. You will hear two psychology students, Priya and Callum, talking to their tutor, Dr Brandt, about a presentation on background music.
Come in, both of you. I've had a look at your slides, but first remind me how you chose your topic. I seem to remember Callum wanted to study sleep.
Yes, that was my first idea. But you told us there's already a huge amount of research on sleep, so we dropped it.
I suggested the music topic, actually. I always study with headphones on and my grades are fine, so I wondered whether music really helps people concentrate.
That's a perfectly good reason to start. Personal curiosity often makes the best research question. Now, tell me about the participants.
We managed to get forty volunteers. Getting them to turn up was easy, because we ran the sessions in the library at lunchtime.
The only real difficulty was that nearly all of them were first-year psychology students. I think that makes our sample rather narrow.
It does, and you should say so on your limitations slide. What task did they do while the music was playing?
We gave them lists of words to memorise and recall afterwards.
Hmm. I'd question that. Your presentation is about concentration, but remembering word lists tests memory more than concentration. A proof-reading task would have suited your aim better.
That's a fair point. We'll mention it in the discussion section.
Good. Now, the results. What did you find for the three conditions: silence, instrumental music and music with lyrics?
I expected instrumental music to help, but the scores were almost identical to silence. The real difference was with lyrics, where people remembered far fewer words.
So instrumental music made little difference, but songs with words clearly got in the way.
That's an interesting pattern, and it fits with earlier studies. Now, let me give you some comments on each part of your presentation.
Your introduction begins with a definition of concentration. That's accurate, but a bit dry. Why not open with a question to the audience, such as who studies with music on?
Oh, I like that. We could ask for a show of hands.
Exactly. For the method, you've written a whole paragraph describing the timing of the sessions. I'd replace that with a simple diagram, because it's much quicker to follow.
I could do that. I thought of a flowchart, or maybe a photo of the room layout. Which would you prefer?
The flowchart. The photo wouldn't tell the audience anything useful.
For the results, you've put all the numbers into a table. A table is fine for the handout, but on the screen a bar graph would show the difference far more clearly.
Right, we'll turn it into a bar graph.
The limitations section currently runs over three slides, which is far too much. Shorten it to a single slide with the main points.
Yes, we did go on a bit there.
And finally the conclusion. It's sensible, but it feels a little abstract. Add a real-life example, perhaps about students studying in cafés, to show why the findings matter.
That's a nice idea, because lots of students do that. We'll add it.
Dr Brandt, we thought about repeating the study with a better task, to fix the problem with the word lists. Is that worth doing?
I wouldn't. You don't have time before the presentation, and you can simply explain the issue. What I'd suggest is a practice run in front of another group first.
That's a good idea. Hannah's group is presenting on the same day, so we could ask them.
Perfect. Ask them to give you honest feedback, especially on timing.
We will. Thank you, Dr Brandt. That's been really helpful.

blocks.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.q: Why did the students choose background music as their topic?
options: Earlier research on it was unclear.
Priya was curious about her own study habits.
It was easy to find volunteers.
questions.explain: Chủ đề ngủ bị bỏ vì đã có quá nhiều nghiên cứu. Priya nói: "I always study with headphones on ... so I wondered whether music really helps people concentrate."

questions.q: What was the main problem with the participants?
options: They could not attend at the same time.
questions.explain: Có 40 người và họ dễ tập hợp; vấn đề là "nearly all of them were first-year psychology students" nên mẫu hẹp.

questions.q: What criticism does Dr Brandt make of the memory task?
options: It was too easy for the volunteers.
It took too long to mark.
It was unsuitable for first-year students.
It measured something different from what they claimed.
questions.explain: Thầy nói: "remembering word lists tests memory more than concentration" — tức đo kỹ năng khác với mục tiêu của bài.

questions.q: What did the results show about instrumental music?
options: It made little difference to scores.
It helped some people but not others.
questions.explain: Callum dự đoán nhạc không lời sẽ giúp nhưng "the scores were almost identical to silence"; chỉ nhạc có lời làm điểm giảm rõ rệt.

questions.q: What does Dr Brandt advise the students to do before the presentation?
options: repeat the study with a better task
practise in front of another group
questions.explain: Thầy bác ý định làm lại nghiên cứu vì không đủ thời gian và đề nghị: "a practice run in front of another group first".

blocks.instructions: What does Dr Brandt suggest for each part of the presentation? Choose FIVE answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–G, next to Questions 26–30.
options: E  move it to the end

questions.explain: Phần mở đầu đúng nhưng khô khan: "Why not open with a question to the audience" (C).
Thay đoạn văn mô tả thời gian bằng sơ đồ: "I'd replace that with a simple diagram"; thầy chọn flowchart chứ không phải ảnh phòng (A).
Bảng số liệu để cho handout; trên màn hình "a bar graph would show the difference far more clearly" (F).
Ba slide là quá nhiều: "Shorten it to a single slide" (B).
Phần kết hơi trừu tượng: "Add a real-life example, perhaps about students studying in cafés" (D).
